claims.text: Wear performance of HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer generated during post-deposition thermal treatment.
The as-deposited HEA coating has a complex multiphase microstructure.
The as-deposited HEA coating has relatively coarse surface features.
Post-deposition thermal treatment can selectively tune the formation and thickness of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer without changing overall alloy composition.
The relevant structural mediator is increased thickness and density of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer at the friction interface.
The refined surface layer enhances accommodation of plastic strain during sliding.
The refined surface layer improves stress distribution and thereby suppresses crack initiation.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer reduces delamination and the severity of adhesive and abrasive wear.
Thermally treated coatings will have lower friction coefficients than untreated as-deposited coatings.
Thermally treated coatings will have lower wear rates than untreated as-deposited coatings.
Wear improvement occurs only over a moderate thermal-treatment range, while excessive treatment that alters bulk properties can negate the benefit.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply at room temperature when adhesive or abrasive wear dominates.
At high temperatures, tribochemical reactions and oxide-scale formation may dominate wear and limit applicability of the proposed mechanism.
Secondary microstructural changes caused by thermal treatment could also contribute to wear behavior.
Wear volume loss can be quantified by topographical interferometric measurement of the wear track.

The hypothesis is falsified if treatment does not significantly reduce both friction coefficient and wear rate, or if equivalent improvements occur without a measurable increase in surface nanocrystallinity.
